articles.title: Thai student movement forms ‘Hope Theatre,’ making the stage its new battleground
articles.summary: “If you’re a bad student in your school, maybe it’s because you’re rebellious. Maybe it’s because you’re brave enough to question your teacher or challenge their power.“
articles.content:
This article by Tara Abhasakun was published by Prachatai, an independent news site in Thailand. An edited version has been republished by Global Voices under a content partnership agreement. It is also part of Global Voices’ September 2026 Spotlight series, “Protest in Democracy.” You can support this coverage by donating here.

This past year, Thailand’s “Bad Student Organization” turned to a new mechanism to question seemingly unbreakable cultural and educational taboos: The theatre.

In 2025, the organization formed Hope Theatre in order to create a dialogue around long-held Thai cultural norms and practices, particularly those involving education and students’ rights. Some of the issues they tackled include corporal punishment, never questioning teachers, mandatory school uniforms, and compliance with haircut regulations.

In September 2025, Hope Theatre delivered its first performance, a musical called “Ribbon Club,” which centered around four students who seek to uncover the truth behind a classmate’s mysterious death at an academy for magic similar to Harry Potter’s Hogwarts. At the behest of Jinny, a top student at the school, students gather to discuss the institution, its rigid rules, how teachers use violence against them, and the identities they are forced to adopt.

As Thamjuthi Thiangtham, 18, who recently completed his freshman year at Chulalongkorn University and works as an editor for the Bad Student Organization, explained, “we started with the question of violence in the context of Thai schools … authoritarianism and violence directed against the lives and freedoms of students.”

He was referring to Thailand’s long-standing use of corporal punishment in schools. It was officially banned in March 2025, but the law has not been strictly enforced. Thamjuthi said that over the past year, his organization received over 200 reports of student rights violations, including corporal punishment, mental abuse, and discrimination against LGBTQ+ students.

Thai teachers still frequently make headlines by imposing physical punishments on students. In June 2025, three months after the ban was implemented, a Bangkok teacher made a student do 200 squats as punishment for late homework. In February 2026, another student was hospitalized after his teacher ordered him to perform 800 squats for failing to submit an assignment.

Raising the issue on stage allowed student actors to address the violence directed again their peers. It also let them magically defend themselves from violent teachers.

Another topic raised during “Ribbon Club,” the musical, is the suppression of classroom questions and debate. In the play, the characters have a special room where they can go for open conversations, similar to the room Harry Potter and his friends secretly gathered in to train against dark magic after a corrupt teacher refused to teach them. It provides a safe space for the students to break free from strict school rules. Inside, they can talk about anything, questioning, challenging, and debating with friends. According to Thamjuthi, it frees them “to openly question the school power structure.”

The room is a plot device which serves to challenge cultural notions of what makes a “good student.” In Thai society, Thamjuthi said, “ideal” students don’t just have academic ability; they obey their teachers and don’t ask questions. “Conversely, a student who is brave enough to ask questions and disagree is considered arrogant … and labeled bad.” However, in the play, when the ‘good’ and ‘bad’ students meet each other and talk in the secret room, they discover there are no differences between them.

In the world of Ribbon Club, it is magic that serves as an indicator of who is a good student. Anything unrelated is deemed useless. Students are expected to use magic every day or — according to an ancient belief — some sort of major disaster will happen. The idea of using magic as a symbol, Thamjuthi said, was meant to help non-Thai audience members who might be less familiar with the context of the Thai education system understand the themes of the play. The audience included members of the Swedish Embassy, as well as some Chinese and American nationals.

According to Thamjuthi, around 80 percent of the audience were young people who already agreed with Hope Theatre’s message and criticisms. The rest were elderly people who agreed with the play’s message but didn’t necessarily support direct protest. Younger audience members thanked the theater group for making them more optimistic and hopeful about change in Thai schools. As for the elderly, although the play “wasn’t polite enough for them,” Hope Theatre’s advocacy drew praise from some, including a very conservative high school principal. Thamjuthi found it impressive that “art has this power to bring people, even those who might not stand on our side, to have more faith in us.”

Hope Theatre’s next performance will likely be staged in late 2026 or early 2027. They haven’t drafted a script yet, but Thamjuthi said it will explore the intense competition to be admitted to Thailand’s top schools. One idea in the works is a reality or game show in which students must fiercely compete to prove their abilities. According to Thamjuthi, “contestants can do anything, no matter if it’s right or wrong, to compete for the prize.”

From the height of Thailand’s youth protests in 2020–2022, the student movement has largely quieted down. In 2020, Bad Student led numerous protests for students’ rights and protections from strict uniform policies, haircut rules, and abusive teachers. Their protests often included costumes and creative expression, such as songs from the Japanese cartoon “Hamtaro.” These protests came amidst a larger protest movement demanding reforms of Thailand’s Article 112, which prohibits criticism of the country’s monarchy. Thamjuthi noted that Bad Student doesn’t engage with national political issues, such as political parties, the constitution, or the justice system. However, regarding the larger protest movement, he remarked that as a result of the government’s ensuing crackdown, “most of our protest leaders had to go overseas … with negative consequences for the movement,” Thamjuthi said.

Thamjuthi remains hopeful for change, despite the election results earlier this year. He notes that “Bad Student” has become a household name throughout the country and no longer carries a negative connotation. “If you’re a bad student in your school, maybe it’s because you’re rebellious. Maybe it’s because you’re brave enough to question your teacher or challenge their power,” he said.

Hope Theatre’s primary challenge, Thamjuthi said, is funding. Last year, the initiative was lucky enough to receive funding from the Swedish International Development Cooperation Agency (SIDA). Now, however, it must find a new source of funding. It is not easy. “To work with students in this society, to work with youth to promote democracy… few funders or businesses are confident enough.”

Hope Theatre is a continuation of the student movement’s focus on art and culture. In the beginning, the organization used dinosaurs to portray conservatives, promoting the slogan “goodbye dinosaurs.” Bad Student has also provided students with cartoon guidebooks to help students understand their rights. Another of their past artistic endeavors involved translating songs from “Matilda” the musical into Thai in order to explain learners’ rights.
articles.reasoning: The article describes a student-led initiative using theatre to challenge authoritarian practices and promote student rights in Thailand, addressing corporal punishment and suppression of free expression in schools. This has broad societal significance as it fosters dialogue on education reform and youth empowerment, with tangible cultural impact and hopeful reception among diverse audiences.
articles.personality_title: Thai students use theatre to challenge school rules and promote rights
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – In Thailand, schools have long been strict places where students must follow many rules, including wearing uniforms, keeping certain haircuts, and not questioning teachers. Corporal punishment was only recently banned but is still common.

**What happened** – In 2025, a student group called the Bad Student Organization created Hope Theatre. They use plays to talk about problems in Thai schools like violence, strict rules, and students’ rights. Their first play, "Ribbon Club," was a musical about students who secretly meet to question unfair school rules and fight back against harsh teachers.

**Impact** – The play gave students a new way to speak out about real issues like punishment and silence in classrooms. It helped audiences, including young people and adults, understand that questioning authority doesn’t make a student bad. The theatre brought attention to student rights and made some adults more open to change.

**What’s next step** – Hope Theatre plans another show for late 2026 or early 2027 about the pressure students face to get into top schools. They want to explore how competition can be unfair and stressful. Meanwhile, they are looking for new funding to keep their work going.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Thai students are using theatre to challenge unfair school rules and inspire conversations about student rights and education reform.
articles.personality_title_fr: Des étudiants thaïlandais utilisent le théâtre pour remettre en question les règles scolaires et défendre leurs droits
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – En Thaïlande, les écoles ont longtemps été des lieux stricts où les élèves doivent suivre de nombreuses règles, comme porter un uniforme, respecter des coupes de cheveux précises et ne pas remettre en question les enseignants. La punition corporelle a été interdite récemment, mais elle reste courante.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – En 2025, un groupe d’étudiants appelé l’Organisation des Mauvais Élèves a créé Hope Theatre. Ils utilisent le théâtre pour parler des problèmes dans les écoles thaïlandaises, comme la violence, les règles strictes et les droits des élèves. Leur première pièce, « Ribbon Club », est une comédie musicale sur des élèves qui se réunissent secrètement pour remettre en question les règles injustes et lutter contre des professeurs sévères.

**Impact** – La pièce a offert aux élèves un nouveau moyen d’exprimer des problèmes réels comme les punitions et le silence en classe. Elle a aidé les spectateurs, jeunes et adultes, à comprendre que poser des questions n’est pas un signe de mauvais élève. Le théâtre a attiré l’attention sur les droits des élèves et a rendu certains adultes plus ouverts au changement.

**Prochaine étape** – Hope Theatre prévoit un nouveau spectacle pour fin 2026 ou début 2027 sur la pression que subissent les élèves pour entrer dans les meilleures écoles. Ils veulent montrer comment la compétition peut être injuste et stressante. En attendant, ils cherchent de nouveaux financements pour continuer leur travail.

**Phrase clé** – Des étudiants thaïlandais utilisent le théâtre pour défier les règles scolaires injustes et encourager le dialogue sur les droits des élèves et la réforme de l’éducation.
articles.personality_title_es: Estudiantes tailandeses usan el teatro para cuestionar las reglas escolares y defender sus derechos
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – En Tailandia, las escuelas han sido durante mucho tiempo lugares estrictos donde los estudiantes deben seguir muchas reglas, como usar uniforme, tener ciertos cortes de cabello y no cuestionar a los profesores. El castigo corporal se prohibió recientemente, pero aún es común.

**Qué pasó** – En 2025, un grupo llamado la Organización de Malos Estudiantes creó Hope Theatre. Usan obras de teatro para hablar sobre problemas en las escuelas tailandesas, como la violencia, las reglas estrictas y los derechos estudiantiles. Su primera obra, "Ribbon Club", fue un musical sobre estudiantes que se reúnen en secreto para cuestionar reglas injustas y enfrentar a profesores duros.

**Impacto** – La obra dio a los estudiantes una nueva forma de expresar problemas reales como el castigo y el silencio en clase. Ayudó a que jóvenes y adultos entendieran que cuestionar la autoridad no hace a un estudiante malo. El teatro llamó la atención sobre los derechos de los estudiantes y abrió a algunos adultos a aceptar cambios.

**Próximo paso** – Hope Theatre planea otro espectáculo para finales de 2026 o principios de 2027 sobre la presión que enfrentan los estudiantes para entrar a las mejores escuelas. Quieren mostrar cómo la competencia puede ser injusta y estresante. Mientras tanto, buscan financiamiento para continuar.

**Frase clave** – Estudiantes tailandeses usan el teatro para desafiar reglas escolares injustas e inspirar conversaciones sobre derechos estudiantiles y reforma educativa.

articles.title: ‘Ask us first’: Children demand a voice on AI’s future
articles.summary: The first generation to grow up with AI may also be the last one anyone thinks to ask about it – and that has to change, the UN's top human rights official said on Tuesday.
articles.content:
“Today's children are the first generation to grow up with artificial intelligence – yet often the last to be asked for their views,” UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk told a high-level meeting in New York on protecting children in the age of AI, held on the sidelines of the General Debate.

Children, he insisted, must be treated as full rights-holders in how AI is built and used – not an afterthought once the technology has already shaped their lives.

The meeting was co-chaired by French President Emmanuel Macron, Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, Kenyan President William Ruto and Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese.

What’s the worry?

Mr. Türk's office, working with partners, surveyed more than 1,000 children across 49 countries.

Their answers paint a sharp picture of unease: fake images made of real people, personal data harvested and exploited, creativity quietly eroded, and a fear that AI could edge out real relationships with family, friends, teachers or therapists.

The throughline was simple. Children want to be heard before the decisions get made and not handed the results afterwards.

Building in safeguards

For Mr. Türk, the answer already exists on paper: the Convention on the Rights of the Child, the most widely ratified human rights treaty in the world, applies just as much to AI as to anything else.

That puts real obligations on the companies building these systems, he said – human rights risk assessments before products ever reach the market, genuine transparency and independent oversight, not self-policing.

Governments, too, have to do more than encourage good behaviour. “Voluntary commitments are not enough,” Mr. Türk warned.

The New York meeting builds on a coalition launched in Geneva in July, another wordy but important grouping known as the Coalition for Children's Rights and Protection in the Age of Artificial Intelligence.

It brings together governments, UN agencies, tech companies, civil society groups and outside experts.

Seventeen countries have signed on so far. Its goal: get children themselves into the room when AI systems that shape their lives are designed, deployed and monitored.

“Children's rights apply to AI," Mr. Türk said, "just as they apply everywhere else.”

Sexualised images proliferate

For Catherine Russell, Executive Director of UNICEF, children are not hanging around waiting for adults to finish defining the rules: they are already using AI, which can offer them important opportunities to learn, create and access information and services.

But the risks are also considerable. According to UN Children’s Fund research, at least 1.2 million children in 11 countries saw their likenesses transformed into AI-generated sexual images during the past year.

She said there was no disguising the damage that AI is already doing to a whole generation of children, Ms. Russell said.
articles.source: UN News - Global perspective Human stories

It reports on a meaningful international coalition involving governments, UN agencies, and civil society to ensure AI development respects children's rights, which has broad societal impact and substance.
articles.personality_title: Children demand a say in how AI affects their lives
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Children today are the first generation to grow up surrounded by artificial intelligence (AI). However, they are often not asked what they think about how AI is being used or how it affects them.

**What happened** – At a meeting in New York, the United Nations (UN) High Commissioner for Human Rights, Volker Türk, said children must be included in decisions about AI. The meeting was led by leaders from France, Spain, Kenya, and Australia. Over 1,000 children from 49 countries shared their concerns about AI, including worries about fake images, misuse of personal data, and losing real connections with people.

**Impact** – This is important because it shows that children want to be part of the conversation before AI technologies are made and used, not after. The UN reminded companies and governments that children’s rights, protected by international laws, must be respected in AI development. This means companies should check for risks and be open about their work, and governments should enforce rules, not just ask companies to behave voluntarily.

**What’s next step** – A group called the Coalition for Children's Rights and Protection in the Age of Artificial Intelligence was created. It includes governments, UN groups, tech companies, and experts. So far, 17 countries have joined. Their goal is to make sure children’s voices are heard when AI systems are designed and used. UNICEF also warns about serious problems, like AI creating harmful images of children, showing why protections are urgently needed.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Children want to be included in decisions about AI to protect their rights and shape a safer future with technology.
articles.personality_title_fr: Les enfants demandent à être consultés sur l'avenir de l'IA
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les enfants d'aujourd'hui sont la première génération à grandir avec l'intelligence artificielle (IA), mais on ne leur demande souvent pas leur avis sur son utilisation ou ses effets.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – Lors d'une réunion à New York, le Haut-Commissaire des Nations Unies aux droits de l'homme, Volker Türk, a déclaré que les enfants doivent être inclus dans les décisions concernant l'IA. La réunion était dirigée par les dirigeants de la France, de l'Espagne, du Kenya et de l'Australie. Plus de 1 000 enfants de 49 pays ont exprimé leurs inquiétudes, notamment sur les images fausses, l'utilisation abusive des données personnelles et la perte de liens réels avec les autres.

**Impact** – Cela montre que les enfants veulent participer à la conversation avant que les technologies d'IA ne soient développées et utilisées, pas après. L'ONU rappelle aux entreprises et aux gouvernements que les droits des enfants, protégés par des lois internationales, doivent être respectés dans le développement de l'IA. Les entreprises doivent évaluer les risques et être transparentes, tandis que les gouvernements doivent faire respecter les règles.

**Prochaine étape** – Une coalition appelée Coalition pour les droits et la protection des enfants à l'ère de l'intelligence artificielle a été créée. Elle rassemble des gouvernements, des agences de l'ONU, des entreprises technologiques et des experts. Dix-sept pays y ont déjà adhéré. Leur but est d'assurer que la voix des enfants soit entendue lors de la conception et de l'utilisation des systèmes d'IA. L'UNICEF alerte aussi sur des problèmes graves, comme la création d'images nuisibles d'enfants par l'IA, ce qui montre l'urgence de protections.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Les enfants veulent être inclus dans les décisions sur l'IA pour protéger leurs droits et construire un avenir technologique plus sûr.
articles.personality_title_es: Los niños exigen tener voz en el futuro de la IA
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Los niños de hoy son la primera generación que crece con inteligencia artificial (IA), pero a menudo no se les pregunta qué piensan sobre su uso o cómo les afecta.

**Qué pasó** – En una reunión en Nueva York, el Alto Comisionado de las Naciones Unidas para los Derechos Humanos, Volker Türk, dijo que los niños deben participar en las decisiones sobre la IA. La reunión fue dirigida por líderes de Francia, España, Kenia y Australia. Más de 1,000 niños de 49 países compartieron sus preocupaciones sobre la IA, incluyendo imágenes falsas, uso indebido de datos personales y la pérdida de conexiones reales con otras personas.

**Impacto** – Esto es importante porque muestra que los niños quieren formar parte de la conversación antes de que las tecnologías de IA se creen y usen, no después. La ONU recordó a las empresas y gobiernos que los derechos de los niños, protegidos por leyes internacionales, deben respetarse en el desarrollo de la IA. Las empresas deben evaluar riesgos y ser transparentes, y los gobiernos deben hacer cumplir las reglas.

**Próximo paso** – Se creó un grupo llamado Coalición para los Derechos y la Protección de los Niños en la Era de la Inteligencia Artificial. Incluye gobiernos, agencias de la ONU, empresas tecnológicas y expertos. Hasta ahora, 17 países se han unido. Su objetivo es asegurar que las voces de los niños se escuchen cuando se diseñen y usen los sistemas de IA. UNICEF también advierte sobre problemas serios, como la creación de imágenes dañinas de niños por IA, mostrando la urgencia de protección.

**Resumen en una frase** – Los niños quieren participar en las decisiones sobre la IA para proteger sus derechos y construir un futuro tecnológico más seguro.

articles.title: Diplomacy is the way to address global challenges, Brazil tells General Assembly
articles.summary: Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva told the General Assembly on Tuesday that the UN needs to become a “temple of peace” once again, as it confronts one of the most critical periods in its 80-year history.
articles.content:
Opening this year’s General Debate, the President – known to all as Lula – expressed his indignation at the widespread attacks taking place on multilateralism worldwide.

According to the Brazilian leader, more effective diplomacy is the only way for collective challenges to be successfully addressed.

He said the organization's credibility has been weakened due to paralysis of the Security Council, the use of veto powers and growing geopolitical tensions.

“We are all held hostage by the inaction of the Security Council” he said, stressing that Brazil has spoken out against the use of veto power by permanent members in the chamber since the first general assembly meeting in 1946.

World of conflict

The Brazilian leader recalled that the previous year had seen the highest number of armed conflicts registered since the Second World War.

He called for regional conflicts to be contained before they escalate into “tragedies of global proportions”.

Turning to the conflict in the Middle East, Lula said that “generations of Palestinians” will now carry “the pain and trauma left by the genocide of women and children,” criticising the expansion of Israeli settlements in the West Bank – all making a two-State solution increasingly difficult to achieve.

Lula also addressed the war between Russia and Ukraine, saying the conflict had continued to claim lives and that there would be “no winners on the battlefield”.

Brazil’s path

He also highlighted key policies at home, noting that Brazil has once again made inroads against hunger and adopted a new law to combat corruption and organised crime – which has led to a record level of seizures of drugs, assets and illicit funds.

“The fight against corruption shall remain relentless," Lula said. "No matter who it hurts. No one is above the law.”

Trusting science

On climate change, President Lula said that, in an era of disinformation, those who reject scientific evidence are denying reality.

He said economic development should always go hand in hand with environmental protection.

The president also called for greater regulation of large technology companies and artificial intelligence (AI), warning against a technological race without ethical safeguards.

In his closing remarks, Lula highlighted the UN's historic role in decolonisation, human rights, sustainable development and the protection of migrants and refugees.

He called on Member States to find the political will to once again make the UN a “temple of peace”
articles.source: UN News - Global perspective Human stories
articles.reasoning: The article highlights Brazil's President Lula advocating for renewed diplomacy, peace, and multilateral cooperation at the UN General Assembly, addressing global conflicts, human rights, anti-corruption efforts, climate action, and ethical technology regulation. This represents a meaningful call for collective action on broad, significant global challenges with potential positive impact on peace, justice, and sustainable development.
articles.personality_title: Brazil’s President Lula urges renewed diplomacy and peace at the UN General Assembly
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – The United Nations (UN) is facing one of its toughest times in over 80 years, with many global conflicts and challenges making it hard for countries to work together.

**What happened** – On Tuesday, Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, known as Lula, spoke at the UN General Assembly. He called for the UN to become a “temple of peace” again and stressed that diplomacy—talking and working together—is the only way to solve big global problems. Lula criticized the Security Council’s lack of action, especially the use of veto power by some members, which stops important decisions. He mentioned recent conflicts, like those in the Middle East and between Russia and Ukraine, and warned that these wars cause great suffering and make peace harder to reach.

**Impact** – Lula’s speech is important because it highlights the need for cooperation and trust among countries during difficult times. He also shared positive news about Brazil fighting corruption, reducing hunger, and protecting the environment. His call for better rules on technology and respect for science shows a plan for a safer future. This message encourages countries to work together for peace, justice, and protecting the planet.

**What’s next step** – Lula wants UN member countries to find the political will, meaning the desire and commitment, to strengthen the UN’s role in solving problems. This could lead to new efforts to limit the use of veto power, increase peace talks, improve laws on technology, and protect human rights and the environment.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Brazil’s President Lula calls for stronger diplomacy and cooperation at the UN to address conflicts, corruption, climate change, and technology challenges for a peaceful future.
articles.personality_title_fr: Le président brésilien Lula appelle à une diplomatie renouvelée et à la paix à l’Assemblée générale de l’ONU
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les Nations Unies (ONU) traversent une période difficile depuis plus de 80 ans, avec de nombreux conflits et défis mondiaux qui compliquent la coopération entre pays.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Mardi, le président brésilien Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, surnommé Lula, a pris la parole à l’Assemblée générale de l’ONU. Il a demandé que l’ONU redevienne un « temple de la paix » et a souligné que la diplomatie – le dialogue et la coopération – est la seule manière de résoudre les grands problèmes mondiaux. Lula a critiqué le Conseil de sécurité pour son inaction, notamment l’usage du droit de veto par certains membres, qui bloque les décisions importantes. Il a évoqué les conflits récents, comme au Moyen-Orient et entre la Russie et l’Ukraine, et a averti que ces guerres causent de grandes souffrances et rendent la paix plus difficile.

**Impact** – Le discours de Lula est important car il souligne la nécessité de coopération et de confiance entre les pays en temps de crise. Il a aussi partagé des nouvelles positives sur le Brésil, qui lutte contre la corruption, réduit la faim et protège l’environnement. Son appel à mieux réglementer la technologie et à respecter la science montre une vision pour un avenir plus sûr. Ce message encourage les pays à travailler ensemble pour la paix, la justice et la protection de la planète.

**Prochaine étape** – Lula souhaite que les États membres de l’ONU trouvent la volonté politique, c’est-à-dire le désir et l’engagement, pour renforcer le rôle de l’ONU dans la résolution des problèmes. Cela pourrait mener à de nouveaux efforts pour limiter l’usage du veto, augmenter les négociations de paix, améliorer les lois sur la technologie et protéger les droits humains et l’environnement.

**Phrase clé** – Le président brésilien Lula appelle à une diplomatie et une coopération renforcées à l’ONU pour faire face aux conflits, à la corruption, au changement climatique et aux défis technologiques en vue d’un avenir pacifique.
articles.personality_title_es: El presidente de Brasil, Lula, pide renovar la diplomacia y la paz en la Asamblea General de la ONU
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Las Naciones Unidas (ONU) enfrentan uno de sus momentos más difíciles en más de 80 años, con muchos conflictos y desafíos globales que dificultan la cooperación entre países.

**Qué pasó** – El martes, el presidente brasileño Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, conocido como Lula, habló en la Asamblea General de la ONU. Pidió que la ONU vuelva a ser un “templo de paz” y destacó que la diplomacia, es decir, hablar y trabajar juntos, es la única forma de resolver grandes problemas globales. Lula criticó la falta de acción del Consejo de Seguridad, especialmente el uso del poder de veto por algunos miembros, que bloquea decisiones importantes. Mencionó conflictos recientes, como en Medio Oriente y entre Rusia y Ucrania, y advirtió que estas guerras causan gran sufrimiento y dificultan la paz.

**Impacto** – El discurso de Lula es importante porque resalta la necesidad de cooperación y confianza entre países en tiempos difíciles. También compartió noticias positivas sobre Brasil, que lucha contra la corrupción, reduce el hambre y protege el medio ambiente.
